intro: A book can tell you what to believe. It can also tell you how to live. The Qur'an does both. This unit looks at what the Qur'an teaches: about one God, about being honest and kind, and about what Muslims do each day and each year because of it.

You will meet a wise man named Luqman and his seven pieces of advice. You will read what the Qur'an says about parents, promises, orphans and boasting. Then you will follow a Muslim child's day and year: the five daily prayers, giving, the month of Ramadan, the journey to Mecca and the two Eid holidays.

Every time, you will see where in the Qur'an an idea comes from, by surah and ayah. You will say "Muslims believe" and "the Qur'an says," so you can describe a faith fairly, whether it is yours or not. By the end you will be able to explain each of the Five Pillars and the verses Muslims point to for them.
bigQuestion: What does the Qur'an ask of Muslims, in belief and in daily life, and where in the book does each teaching come from?

test.q: Which surah do Muslims say sums up the idea of one God in four short ayahs?
test.why: Surah 112, Al-Ikhlas, says God is one, needs nothing, has no children and has no equal.

test.q: How does the Qur'an describe paradise in 2:25?
test.why: 2:25 describes gardens with rivers flowing beneath and fruit.

test.why: The Five Pillars are the shahada, daily prayer, zakat, fasting in Ramadan and the hajj.

test.q: What does Surah 2:144 tell Muslims to do?

test.why: 2:144 sets the qibla: face the Sacred Mosque in Mecca in prayer.

test.q: Who does Surah 2:185 say may fast on other days instead of in Ramadan?
test.why: 2:185 says the sick and those on a journey may make up the fast on other days.

test.q: What does 3:97 say about the journey to the Kaaba?
choices: It must be made every Friday
It is only for people from Arabia
It is a duty for those who are able to make the trip

write.prompt: What does the Qur'an say a good person does? Pick two or three passages from this unit, such as 17:23–24 on parents, 2:177 on giving, 31:13–19 on Luqman's advice or 2:185 on fasting. For each, tell what the passage says in your own words, and how Muslims put it into practice.
tips: Name each passage by surah and ayah, like 2:177.
Say "the Qur'an says" or "Muslims believe" every time; describe, do not judge.
Use the unit's words: tawhid, zakat, qibla, Ramadan, halal.
Give one example of how a Muslim family might follow each passage.
Keep your sentences short and say one idea in each.

title: What the Qur'an Teaches

chapters.title: One God, and Being Good
chapters.bigQuestion: What does the Qur'an say about God, and about how a person should treat others?

story.title: A Walk with Luqman
story.kicker: A wise man walks with his son and gives him seven pieces of advice.
paragraphs: The sun is going down over a dusty road. A father and his son walk side by side. The father's name is Luqman. Muslims remember him as a wise man. The Qur'an gives a whole surah his name, Surah 31, Luqman.
Luqman does not give his son a toy or a coin. He gives him advice. He speaks slowly, one idea at a time. "My dear son," he begins. The boy listens. The road is quiet, and every word counts.

The first advice is the biggest. Luqman tells his son that there is only one God. Then he speaks of small things too. Be kind to your parents. Do not turn your face away from people in scorn. Do not walk with a proud strut. Speak in a soft voice.

The Qur'an tells this walk in seven short ayahs, 31:13 to 31:19. Muslims have read them to children for over a thousand years. Many families still do. They say the advice is as good today as it was long ago.

In this chapter you will read what the Qur'an says about one God. You will read what it says about being honest, keeping promises and caring for others. And you will meet Luqman's seven pieces of advice, one by one.
story.think: If you could give one piece of advice to a younger child, what would it be, and why?

lessons.title: One God, Not Many
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe there is only one God, and the Qur'an calls this idea tawhid.
reading: Long ago in Mecca, people prayed to many gods. Statues stood around the Kaaba, the square building in the middle of the city. Muslims believe the Qur'an came to change this. Its biggest message is short: there is only one God.

The Arabic word for this idea is *tawhid*. It means "making one" or "oneness." Muslims believe God made everything, God has no partner and nothing is like God. The Qur'an says it again and again, in long surahs and in short ones.

One tiny surah says it best. Surah 112, Al-Ikhlas, has only four ayahs. Muslims believe it sums up the whole idea of one God. Many Muslim children learn it by heart when they are very young. You will read it in the next lesson.

words.d: the belief that there is only one God; the Qur'an's central idea
the square building in Mecca that Muslims face when they pray

look.title: Before and After
look.text: Picture Mecca before Islam. Around the Kaaba stand many statues, one for each god a family or tribe prays to. Now picture the same place after the Qur'an's message. The statues are gone. People say there is one God only. What changed is not the building. It is the idea.
look.prompt: In your own words, what does tawhid mean, and what did it change about Mecca?

check.q: What does the word tawhid mean?
choices: The belief that there is only one God
The name of a city in Arabia
check.why: Tawhid means oneness: the belief that there is only one God, the Qur'an's central idea.

check.q: Before Islam, what stood around the Kaaba in Mecca?
check.why: Muslim tradition says that many statues of gods stood around the Kaaba before the Qur'an's message.

check.q: Which surah do Muslims say sums up the idea of one God in four ayahs?
check.why: Surah 112, Al-Ikhlas, has four short ayahs about God being one.

lessons.title: Surah Al-Ikhlas Close Up
lessons.mainIdea: Surah 112 says God is one, needs nothing, has no children and has no equal.
reading: Surah 112 is called Al-Ikhlas. The name means "sincerity" or "pure faith." It is near the very end of the Qur'an. It is so short you can read it in one breath. Muslims say it many times a day in prayer.

The surah says four things. God is one. God needs nothing, but everything needs God. God was not born and did not have children. Nothing is like God. Each *ayah* is one idea. An ayah is a line, or verse, of the Qur'an.

Muslims believe this surah answers a question people asked Muhammad: "What is your God like?" The answer does not describe a shape or a face. It says what God is not like. Muslims say that is the point: God is not like anything we can picture.

words.d: one line or verse of the Qur'an; the plural is ayat
Surah 112, a four-line surah about God being one; the name means sincerity

look.title: Surah 112 in an Old Translation
look.text: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him.
look.cite: Qur'an 112:1–4, Al-Ikhlas, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: "Begetteth" is an old word for "has a child." Which of the four lines says God has no children?

check.q: What does the name Al-Ikhlas mean?
check.why: Al-Ikhlas means sincerity or pure faith; it is the name of Surah 112.

check.q: How many ayahs does Surah 112 have?
check.why: Surah Al-Ikhlas has four ayahs; 114 is the number of surahs in the whole Qur'an.

check.q: What is an ayah?
choices: A whole chapter of the Qur'an
One line or verse of the Qur'an
A person who reads the Qur'an
check.why: An ayah is one line or verse; a surah is the whole chapter.

lessons.title: The 99 Names
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims call God by many names from the Qur'an, and the best known are the Merciful and the Kind.
reading: Muslims believe God has many names. Each name tells one thing about God. The Qur'an says that the most beautiful names belong to God, and that people may call on God by them (7:180, Al-A'raf). Muslim tradition counts 99 names.

The two names heard most are Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim. They mean the Most Gracious and the Most *Merciful*. Both come from a root word that means mercy. Nearly every surah opens with them, in the line called the Bismillah.

Other names are the Kind, the Just, the Creator, the Wise and the Giver of Peace. Some Muslims learn all 99 by heart. Some count them on a string of beads. The names are found in the Qur'an, but the list of 99 comes from later Muslim tradition.

words.d: full of mercy; forgiving and gentle toward others
the line "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" that opens nearly every surah

look.title: Counting in the Qur'an
rows: Names of God in Muslim tradition
look.cite: Standard Cairo edition of the Qur'an (1924); the 99 names as counted in Muslim tradition (hadith in the collection of al-Tirmidhi)
look.prompt: Which is bigger: the number of surahs or the number of names? By how many?

check.q: How many names of God does Muslim tradition count?
check.why: Muslim tradition counts 99 names of God; 114 is the number of surahs.

check.q: What do Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim mean?
choices: The Giver of Peace and the Strong
The Most Gracious and the Most Merciful
check.why: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim mean the Most Gracious and the Most Merciful; both come from the root for mercy.

check.q: Where are these two names heard most often?
choices: In the Bismillah at the start of nearly every surah
Only on the Day of Judgment
check.why: The Bismillah, which opens nearly every surah, names God the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

lessons.title: Honor Your Parents
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an tells people to be good to their parents, especially when the parents grow old.
reading: Right after telling people to worship one God, the Qur'an often adds a second rule. Be good to your parents. In Surah 17, Al-Isra, ayahs 23 and 24, the two ideas sit side by side. Muslims say this shows how important parents are.

The passage speaks about parents who grow old. It says not to say even a small word of anger to them. It says to speak to them with *respect*. It says to be humble and gentle, and to pray for them, because they cared for you when you were small.

Muslim children often learn a short prayer from this ayah. It asks God to have mercy on their parents. Many Muslims say it every day. The Qur'an does not say parents are always right. It says to treat them with kindness.

words.d: treating someone as important and worthy of care
not proud; not thinking you are better than others

look.title: Two Rules Together
look.text: Your Lord has ordered that you worship no one but God, and that you be kind to your parents. If one or both of them grow old with you, do not say even "ugh" to them, and do not scold them. Speak to them with kind words. Be gentle and humble with them, and say: My Lord, have mercy on them, as they cared for me when I was little.
look.cite: Qur'an 17:23–24, Al-Isra, paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation (1930)
look.prompt: The passage names one thing not to do and several things to do. List them.

check.q: In 17:23, what rule comes right after "worship no one but God"?
check.why: Surah 17:23 puts kindness to parents right after worship of one God.

check.q: What does the passage say about parents who grow old?
choices: Do not say even a small angry word to them
check.why: The ayah says not to say even a small word of anger to old parents and to speak to them kindly.

check.q: What does humble mean?
choices: Not proud; not thinking you are better than others
check.why: Humble means not proud; the Qur'an asks children to be humble and gentle with their parents.

lessons.title: Honest Words, Kept Promises
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says to tell the truth, give fair measure and keep every promise you make.
reading: The Qur'an says a lot about honesty. It tells people to speak the truth even when it is hard. It tells sellers to give a full measure and a fair weight. Surah 83, Al-Mutaffifin, warns people who cheat when they weigh things for others.

The Qur'an also says to keep a *promise*. In Surah 17:34 it says to be true to every promise, because a person will be asked about it. In Surah 2:177 it praises people who keep their word when they give it. Muslims believe God sees every promise made.

Muslim tradition says people in Mecca called Muhammad al-Amin, "the *trustworthy*," before he ever spoke of the Qur'an. They trusted him to keep things safe. Muslims say this is why honesty matters so much in their faith.

words.d: a word you give that you will do something; the Qur'an says to keep it
someone people can trust; the name al-Amin that Mecca gave Muhammad

look.title: The Short Weight
look.text: A seller in a market has a scale. When a person buys grain, the seller puts a little less on the scale than the buyer paid for. When the seller buys grain from a farmer, he asks for a little extra. Surah 83 opens by warning people who do this. It says they take full measure for themselves but give less to others.
look.prompt: Why do you think the Qur'an treats a small cheat on a scale as a big wrong?

check.q: What does Surah 83, Al-Mutaffifin, warn against?
choices: Cheating when weighing things for others
check.why: Surah 83 warns people who give short measure when they sell but take full measure when they buy.

check.q: What does Surah 17:34 say about promises?
choices: Be true to every promise; you will be asked about it
Promises can be broken on Fridays
check.why: 17:34 says to keep every promise, because a person will be asked about it.

check.q: What name did people in Mecca give Muhammad, according to Muslim tradition?
check.why: Muslim tradition says Mecca called Muhammad al-Amin, the trustworthy, for his honesty.

lessons.title: Orphans and the Poor
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says again and again to care for orphans, the poor and travelers in need.
reading: An *orphan* is a child whose parents have died. Muslim tradition says Muhammad was an orphan himself. His father died before he was born, and his mother died when he was small. The Qur'an speaks about orphans many times.

Surah 93, Ad-Duha, says: do not treat the orphan harshly, and do not push away the one who asks for help. Surah 107, Al-Ma'un, says a person who pushes the orphan away and does not feed the poor is not truly good. Muslims read these as strong words.

Surah 2:177 gives a list of what being good looks like. It says to give money you love to relatives, orphans, the poor, the traveler and those who ask. Muslims believe that giving is not extra. It is part of being a good person.

words.d: a child whose parents have died
a person on a journey, far from home; the Qur'an says to help one in need

look.title: What Goodness Looks Like
look.text: Being good is not just turning your face east or west. The good person believes in God and the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets. That person gives money, though they love it, to relatives, orphans, the poor, the traveler and those who ask. That person prays, gives to the poor, keeps promises, and stays patient in hard times.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:177, Al-Baqarah, paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation (1930)
look.prompt: Count the groups of people this ayah says to give to. Who is on the list?

check.q: What is an orphan?
choices: A child who lives far away
A child whose parents have died
check.why: An orphan is a child whose parents have died; the Qur'an tells people to care for orphans.

check.q: Which surah says not to treat the orphan harshly and not to push away the one who asks?
check.why: Surah 93, Ad-Duha, gives these two commands near its end.

check.q: According to Muslim tradition, why might Muhammad have cared so much about orphans?
check.why: Muslim tradition says Muhammad lost his father before birth and his mother as a small child.

lessons.title: Do Not Boast
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says not to brag, not to strut, and not to look down on other people.
reading: To *boast* means to brag, to talk big about yourself. The Qur'an says God does not love boasters. In Surah 31:18, Luqman tells his son not to turn his cheek away from people in scorn. He tells him not to walk with a proud strut on the earth.

Surah 17:37 says something like it. It says not to walk on the earth proudly, because you cannot split the ground open or grow as tall as the mountains. Muslims read this as a gentle joke. A proud person is still just a person.

Surah 49:11 adds another rule. Do not make fun of other people, and do not call them mean names. The people you laugh at may be better than you. Muslims say a good person is *modest*: quiet about their own good points.

words.d: to brag or talk big about yourself
not showing off; quiet about your own good points

look.title: Two Ways to Walk
look.text: Picture two students walking into the lunchroom. One walks with his chin up, pushing past smaller kids, and turns his face away when someone says hello. The other walks at an easy pace, says hello back and sits with anyone. Surah 31:18 describes the first way of walking and says not to do it.
look.prompt: Which student is boasting without saying a word? What could he do differently?

check.q: What does boast mean?
choices: To brag or talk big about yourself
check.why: To boast is to brag; the Qur'an says God does not love boasters.

check.q: What does Surah 17:37 say a proud walker cannot do?
choices: Split the ground or grow as tall as the mountains
check.why: 17:37 says a proud person cannot split the earth or reach the height of the mountains.

check.q: What does Surah 49:11 say not to do?
choices: Make fun of people or call them mean names
check.why: 49:11 says not to mock others or call them by hurtful names.

lessons.title: A Father and a Son
lessons.mainIdea: Surah 31 tells how the wise man Luqman gave his son advice, and Muslims read it as a lesson for all children.
reading: Surah 31 is named for Luqman. The Qur'an says God gave Luqman *wisdom*, the skill of knowing what is right and doing it. Muslim tradition tells many stories about him. Some say he was from Africa. Some say he was a carpenter or a shepherd. The Qur'an does not say.

In ayahs 13 to 19, Luqman speaks to his son. He calls him "my dear son." He is not angry. He is teaching. Muslims point out that the Qur'an chose a father talking to a child, not a king giving orders, to teach these lessons.

The first thing Luqman says is the biggest: do not set up any partner with God. The Qur'an calls that a great wrong. Muslims say the rest of the advice grows out of this first idea. If God is one, then be humble before God and kind to people.

words.d: knowing what is right and doing it; the Qur'an says God gave this to Luqman
a wise man in the Qur'an who gave his son advice; Surah 31 is named for him

look.title: The First Advice
look.text: Remember when Luqman said to his son, while he was teaching him: My dear son, do not set up partners with God. To set up partners with God is a great wrong.
look.cite: Qur'an 31:13, Luqman, paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation (1930)
look.prompt: What does Luqman call his son? What does that tell you about how he is speaking?

check.q: What does the Qur'an say God gave Luqman?
check.why: Surah 31:12 says God gave Luqman wisdom.

check.q: Who is Luqman speaking to in ayahs 13 to 19?
check.why: Luqman gives his advice to his son, calling him "my dear son."

check.q: What is the first thing Luqman tells his son?
choices: Do not set up partners with God
check.why: 31:13 begins with the biggest idea: there is one God, and setting up partners with God is a great wrong.

lessons.title: Seven Pieces of Advice
lessons.mainIdea: Luqman's advice covers one God, parents, prayer, doing right, patience, not boasting and a soft voice.
reading: Here are Luqman's seven pieces of advice, in simple words. One: worship one God only. Two: be good to your parents. Three: know that God sees even a tiny thing, small as a mustard seed. Four: keep up your prayer.

Five: tell people to do right and stop wrong, and be *patient* when hard things happen. Six: do not turn away from people in scorn or walk proudly. Seven: walk at an easy pace and keep your voice low. The Qur'an adds that the loudest voice of all is the donkey's.

Many Muslims say this list is a whole way of life in seven lines. Teachers in Muslim schools use it. Parents read it at bedtime. Some readers note that the advice moves from God, to family, to how you act with strangers on the street.

words.d: able to wait or bear hard things without complaining
a very tiny seed; the Qur'an uses it as a picture of something small

look.title: The Last Advice
look.text: Be modest in thy bearing and subdue thy voice. Lo! the harshest of all voices is the voice of the ass.
look.cite: Qur'an 31:19, Luqman, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: "Subdue thy voice" means keep your voice low. Why might a wise father end his advice with this?

check.q: How small is the thing the Qur'an says God can see, in Luqman's advice?
choices: As small as a mustard seed
check.why: 31:16 says that even something as small as a mustard seed is known to God.

check.q: What does patient mean?
choices: Able to bear hard things without complaining
check.why: Patient means bearing hard things calmly; Luqman tells his son to be patient when trouble comes.

check.q: What animal's voice does Surah 31:19 call the harshest?
check.why: 31:19 says the harshest of voices is the voice of the donkey, as a picture of a loud, boastful voice.

lessons.title: Angels
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe in angels, and the Qur'an names Jibril (Gabriel), who Muslims believe brought its words.
reading: The Qur'an speaks about *angels*. Muslims believe angels are beings God made from light. They do not eat or sleep. They do what God tells them. Surah 2:177 lists belief in angels as part of being a good person.

The angel named most is Jibril (Gabriel). Muslims believe Jibril brought the words of the Qur'an to Muhammad, a little at a time, over about 23 years. Surah 2:97 names Jibril. Another angel, Mikail (Michael), is named in 2:98.

Muslim tradition also speaks of angels who write down what each person does. The Qur'an mentions two watchers in 50:17–18. Many Muslims picture them on the right and left shoulder. Muslims believe angels exist; other people believe differently, and both study the text.

words.d: a being that Muslims believe God made from light to carry out God's commands
the angel Gabriel; Muslims believe he brought the Qur'an's words to Muhammad

look.title: Two Writers
look.text: Surah 50:17–18 describes two angels who sit, one on the right and one on the left, and write down every word a person says. Many Muslim children are told about them. Some readers say the picture is meant to help a person think before speaking. Others read it as a simple description of what Muslims believe happens.
look.prompt: How might a person act differently if they believed every word was being written down?

check.q: What do Muslims believe angels are made from?
check.why: Muslim tradition says God made angels from light.

check.q: Which angel do Muslims believe brought the Qur'an's words to Muhammad?
check.why: Muslims believe Jibril (Gabriel), named in 2:97, brought the words of the Qur'an.

check.q: Over about how many years do Muslims believe the Qur'an came?
check.why: Muslim tradition says the Qur'an came a little at a time over about 23 years.

lessons.title: The Day of Judgment and Paradise
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe that one day every person will answer for what they did, and that good people will live in paradise.
reading: The Qur'an speaks often about a *Day of Judgment*. Muslims believe that on that day every person will stand before God. Each one will answer for the good and bad they did. The Qur'an says a scale will weigh people's deeds (21:47, Al-Anbiya).

Muslims believe good people will go to *paradise*. The Qur'an describes it as gardens with rivers flowing under them, cool shade and fruit (for example, 2:25). It also describes a place of fire for people who did wrong and never turned back.

The Qur'an also says God is forgiving. Surah 39:53 says people should not lose hope in God's mercy. Muslims believe a person can say sorry and change at any time. Christians and Jews also have beliefs about a judgment and an afterlife, told in their own ways.

words.d: the day Muslims believe every person will answer to God for what they did
the garden where Muslims believe good people will live after death

look.title: A Garden with Rivers
look.text: Give good news to those who believe and do good: for them there are gardens with rivers flowing beneath. Whenever they are given fruit there, they will say, this is like what we were given before. They will have pure partners there, and they will stay there forever.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:25, Al-Baqarah, paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation (1930)
look.prompt: What three things does this description of paradise mention? Why might rivers matter to people in a desert?

check.q: What do Muslims believe happens on the Day of Judgment?
choices: Every person answers to God for what they did
The Qur'an is written for the first time
check.why: Muslims believe every person will stand before God and answer for their deeds.

check.q: How does the Qur'an describe paradise in 2:25?
check.why: 2:25 describes gardens with rivers flowing beneath and fruit.

check.q: What does Surah 39:53 say about God's mercy?
choices: It is only for people in Mecca
Do not lose hope in it
check.why: 39:53 tells people not to lose hope in God's mercy; Muslims believe a person can always turn back.

review.q: What is the Qur'an's central idea about God, called tawhid?
choices: God has many helpers who are also gods
review.why: Tawhid is the belief that there is only one God; the 99 are names, not gods.

review.q: Which surah is named for a wise man who gave his son advice?
review.why: Surah 31 is named Luqman, after the wise man whose advice to his son it tells.

review.q: In 17:23–24, what does the Qur'an say about old parents?
choices: Send them to live in Mecca
Speak to them only in Arabic
Do not say even a small angry word; speak to them kindly
review.why: 17:23–24 says not to say even a small angry word to old parents and to be gentle with them.

review.q: Which surah warns people who cheat with weights and measures?
review.why: Surah 83 opens by warning those who give short measure to others.

review.q: What does Surah 2:177 say a good person does with money?
choices: Gives it to relatives, orphans, the poor and travelers
review.why: 2:177 lists giving to relatives, orphans, the poor, the traveler and those who ask.

review.q: What did Luqman tell his son about his voice?
review.why: 31:19 tells the son to keep his voice low; the harshest voice is the donkey's.

review.q: Who do Muslims believe brought the Qur'an's words to Muhammad?
review.why: Muslims believe Jibril (Gabriel) brought the words of the Qur'an over about 23 years.

review.q: What does the Qur'an say will weigh people's deeds on the Day of Judgment?
review.why: 21:47 says a scale will weigh deeds on the Day of Judgment; the mustard seed is a picture of something small.

chapters.title: Prayer, Fasting and the Pillars in the Qur'an
chapters.bigQuestion: What do Muslims do because of the Qur'an, and where in the book do those practices come from?

story.title: The New Moon over Chicago
story.kicker: The first crescent moon of Ramadan is spotted, and phones light up across the city.
paragraphs: It is just after sunset on the west side of Chicago. Hana stands on the back porch with her father. They are looking at the sky. Not for stars. They are looking for a thin sliver of moon, thin as a fingernail clipping.

Muslims use a calendar that follows the moon. A new month begins when the new crescent moon is seen. The month of Ramadan is the month of fasting. So on this night, families all over the world are doing what Hana is doing: looking up.

Then her father's phone buzzes. Then her mother's. Then the neighbor's, across the fence. A mosque in the city has announced it. The moon has been seen. Ramadan begins tomorrow. Hana's little brother runs through the house shouting, "It's Ramadan!"

Hana is ten. This year she plans to fast for a few days, the way her cousin did. That means no food or drink from dawn to sunset. Her parents say she does not have to. The Qur'an says children, the sick and travelers do not need to fast. But she wants to try.

Tonight the kitchen fills with the smell of dates and soup. Tomorrow, before the sun comes up, the family will eat a quiet breakfast in the dark. In this chapter you will learn why, and what the Qur'an says about prayer, giving, fasting and the journey to Mecca.
story.think: Hana's family found out about Ramadan from the sky and from a phone. What is one thing your family waits for and gets ready for each year?

lessons.title: Five Pillars Hold Up a House
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims describe five main practices as pillars, and each one has roots in the Qur'an.
reading: A *pillar* is a strong post that holds up a roof. Muslims use this word for five main practices of their faith. They call them the Five Pillars. The list comes from a saying of Muhammad in Muslim tradition (a hadith). The Qur'an speaks of each one.

Here are the five. Say the shahada, the short statement of faith. Pray five times a day. Give zakat, a share of one's money, to people in need. Fast in the month of Ramadan. Make the hajj, the journey to Mecca, once in a lifetime if you are able.

Sunni Muslims usually list these five. Shia Muslims list the same practices but often group them a little differently. In this chapter you will meet each pillar and find the ayahs Muslims point to for it.

words.d: a strong post that holds up a roof; Muslims use it for five main practices
a saying or action of Muhammad, remembered and written down by Muslims

look.title: The Pillars by the Numbers
rows: Times a person must make hajj, if able
Words in the shahada, in Arabic, about
look.cite: The Five Pillars as listed in the hadith collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim (9th century), paraphrased
look.prompt: Which pillar is done most often? Which is done least often?

check.q: What is a pillar?
choices: A strong post that holds up a roof
check.why: A pillar holds up a roof; Muslims use the word for five main practices that hold up their faith.

check.q: Where does the list of Five Pillars come from?
choices: A saying of Muhammad in Muslim tradition
check.why: The list of five comes from a hadith, a saying of Muhammad; the Qur'an speaks of each practice.

check.q: Which of these is one of the Five Pillars?
check.why: Fasting in Ramadan is one of the Five Pillars, along with the shahada, prayer, zakat and hajj.

lessons.title: The Shahada: Words of Faith
lessons.mainIdea: The shahada says there is no god but God and Muhammad is God's messenger, and saying it makes a person a Muslim.
reading: The first pillar is the *shahada*. The word means "witness" or "statement." It is one sentence: "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God." Muslims believe a person who says it, and means it, is a Muslim.

The two halves come from the Qur'an. Surah 47:19 says to know that there is no god but God. Surah 48:29 says that Muhammad is the messenger of God. The shahada puts the two ideas together. It makes one short line.

Muslims say the shahada many times. It is in the call to prayer. It is said in every prayer. Many Muslim parents whisper it into a newborn baby's ear. Muslims hope to say it as their last words. It ties the idea of one God to the *messenger* who Muslims believe brought the Qur'an.

words.d: the statement of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God
a person who carries a message; Muslims believe Muhammad carried God's message

look.title: Two Halves, One Sentence
look.text: Half one: "There is no god but God." Half two: "Muhammad is the messenger of God." Muslims say the first half is about who God is. The second half is about how they believe God's words reached people. Jews and Christians would agree with much of the first half, in their own words. The second half is the part that makes a person a Muslim.
look.prompt: Which half of the shahada is about God, and which half is about Muhammad? Why do Muslims say both are needed?

check.q: What does the word shahada mean?
check.why: Shahada means witness or statement; it is the statement of faith.

check.q: Which ayah says there is no god but God?
check.why: Surah 47:19 says: know that there is no god but God.

check.q: When is the shahada often first said to a Muslim?
choices: On the first day of school
check.why: Many Muslim parents whisper the shahada into a newborn's ear.

lessons.title: Prayer Five Times a Day
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims pray five times a day facing Mecca, and the Qur'an tells them to keep up prayer and which way to face.
reading: The second pillar is *salah*, the daily prayer. Muslims pray five times a day: before sunrise, midday, afternoon, sunset and night. The Qur'an says to keep up prayer many times, for example in 2:43 and 2:110. It speaks of prayer at the two ends of the day and at night (11:114).

The names of the five prayers and their exact times come from Muslim tradition, not straight from the Qur'an. Muslims say Muhammad showed how to pray, and his companions passed it on. The prayer has standing, bowing and touching the forehead to the ground.

Muslims all face the same way when they pray: toward the Kaaba in Mecca. This direction is the *qibla*. Surah 2:144 tells Muslims to turn their faces toward the sacred mosque in Mecca. In a mosque, a small arch in the wall shows which way that is.

words.d: the Muslim daily prayer, done five times a day
the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which Muslims face when they pray

look.title: Which Way to Face
look.text: We see you turning your face toward the sky. So We will turn you toward a direction of prayer that will please you. Turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:144, Al-Baqarah, paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation (1930)
look.prompt: In Chicago, the qibla is roughly toward the northeast. Why is it the same direction for a whole city, but different for a city in India?

check.q: How many times a day do Muslims pray?
check.why: Muslims pray five times a day: before sunrise, midday, afternoon, sunset and night.

check.q: What is the qibla?
choices: The direction of the Kaaba in Mecca
check.why: The qibla is the direction Muslims face in prayer, toward the Kaaba in Mecca, as 2:144 says.

check.q: Where do the names and exact times of the five prayers come from?
check.why: The Qur'an says to keep up prayer; the five names and times come from Muhammad's example in Muslim tradition.

lessons.title: Zakat: Giving a Share
lessons.mainIdea: Zakat is a share of one's savings given each year to people in need, and the Qur'an often pairs it with prayer.
reading: The third pillar is *zakat*. The word means "to make pure" or "to grow." Zakat is a share of a person's savings given each year to people in need. Muslims believe giving makes the rest of their money clean.

The Qur'an names prayer and zakat together many times, such as in 2:43: keep up prayer and give zakat. Surah 9:60 lists who may receive it: the poor, the needy, people in debt, travelers and others. Muslims say zakat is a duty, not a gift.

How much? Muslim tradition sets it at about one fortieth of a person's savings, if they have more than a certain amount. Children and the poor do not pay. Giving more than zakat is called *sadaqah*, a free gift. The Qur'an praises this kind of giving too.

words.d: a share of savings that Muslims give each year to people in need; the third pillar
any extra giving beyond zakat; a free gift to someone in need

look.title: One Coin in Forty
look.text: Imagine you have saved forty coins over a year. Muslim tradition says zakat is one coin out of every forty. So you would give one coin to someone in need and keep thirty-nine. If you had four hundred coins, you would give ten. Someone with only a few coins gives none, and may receive zakat instead.
look.prompt: If a family saved eight hundred coins, how many would zakat be? Why do you think the share is the same for everyone who pays?

check.q: What is zakat?
choices: A share of savings given to people in need
check.why: Zakat is a yearly share of savings given to those in need; it is the third pillar.

check.q: Which ayah lists the people who may receive zakat?
check.why: Surah 9:60 lists the poor, the needy, people in debt, travelers and others.

check.q: What is sadaqah?
check.why: Sadaqah is any free gift beyond the required zakat.

lessons.title: Fasting in Ramadan
lessons.mainIdea: Surah 2:185 names Ramadan as the month the Qur'an came down, and tells Muslims to fast in it.
reading: The fourth pillar is fasting in *Ramadan*. Ramadan is the ninth month of the Muslim calendar. Muslims believe it is the month when the Qur'an first came down. For the whole month, adult Muslims do not eat or drink from dawn until sunset.

Surah 2:183 says fasting is prescribed for Muslims, as it was for people before them. Surah 2:185 names the month of Ramadan and says whoever is present in it should fast. It adds that the sick and travelers may make up the days later. It says God wants ease, not hardship.

Each evening families break the fast, often with dates and water first. This meal is called *iftar*. Before dawn they eat again. Many Muslims read one part of the Qur'an each night, so they finish all thirty parts by the end of the month. Ramadan ends with a holiday, Eid al-Fitr.

words.d: the ninth month of the Muslim calendar, when Muslims fast from dawn to sunset
the evening meal that breaks the fast in Ramadan

look.title: The Month of the Qur'an
look.text: The month of Ramadan is the month in which the Qur'an was sent down, as a guide for people and clear proof of guidance. Whoever of you is present in that month should fast in it. Whoever is sick or on a journey may fast the same number of other days. God wants things to be easy for you, not hard.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:185, Al-Baqarah, paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation (1930)
look.prompt: The ayah gives a rule and then two exceptions. What are they? What reason does it give at the end?

check.q: Which month of the Muslim calendar is Ramadan?
check.why: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Muslim calendar.

check.q: According to 2:185, who may fast on other days instead?
check.why: 2:185 says the sick and those on a journey may make up the days later.

check.q: What is iftar?
choices: The evening meal that breaks the fast
check.why: Iftar is the evening meal that breaks the day's fast, often begun with dates and water.

lessons.title: Hajj: The Journey to Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims who are able travel to Mecca once in their lives for the hajj, which the Qur'an calls a duty to God.
reading: The fifth pillar is the *hajj*, the journey to Mecca. Surah 3:97 says that going to the House, the Kaaba, is a duty people owe to God, if they are able to make the trip. Muslims who can afford it and are healthy try to go once in their lives.

The hajj happens in the last month of the Muslim calendar. Millions of people come. They all wear simple white cloth so that no one looks rich or poor. They walk around the Kaaba seven times. They stand together on a plain called Arafat.

Muslims connect the hajj to Ibrahim (Abraham). The Qur'an says Ibrahim and his son Ismail raised the walls of the Kaaba (2:127). Muslims retell his story as they walk. The hajj ends with the holiday of Eid al-Adha, which Muslims all over the world share.

words.d: the journey to Mecca that Muslims make once in a lifetime, if they are able; the fifth pillar
a plain near Mecca where pilgrims stand together on the main day of the hajj

look.title: Everyone in White
look.text: Picture a crowd of two million people. A doctor from Chicago stands next to a farmer from Indonesia and a bus driver from Nigeria. All three wear the same two plain white cloths. No one can tell who is rich. They walk in the same circle around the same square building. Muslims say this is one of the main lessons of the hajj.
look.prompt: Why do you think everyone on the hajj dresses the same? What lesson do Muslims take from it?

check.q: Which ayah calls the journey to the Kaaba a duty for those who are able?
check.why: Surah 3:97 says the journey to the House is a duty owed to God by those who can make it.

check.q: Which prophet do Muslims connect with building the Kaaba?
check.why: The Qur'an in 2:127 says Ibrahim and Ismail raised the walls of the Kaaba.

check.q: Why do pilgrims on the hajj all wear simple white cloth?
choices: Because white is cool in the heat
Because it is a law in Mecca
Because they must sleep in it
So that no one looks rich or poor
check.why: The plain white dress shows that all pilgrims are equal; no one can tell who is rich.

lessons.title: Washing Up and the Mosque
lessons.mainIdea: Before prayer Muslims wash in a set way called wudu, which Surah 5:6 describes, and many pray together in a mosque.
reading: Before praying, Muslims wash. This washing is called *wudu*. Surah 5:6 describes it: wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. If there is no water, the ayah says clean earth may be used instead.

Muslims can pray almost anywhere that is clean: at home, at school, at work, even in an airport. Many also pray together in a *mosque*. The Arabic word is masjid, "a place of bowing down." People take off their shoes at the door.

Inside a mosque there are no chairs and no statues. The floor is covered with carpet. A small arch in one wall shows the qibla. Many mosques have a tall tower called a minaret, from which the call to prayer is given. Chicago has dozens of mosques, large and small.

words.d: the washing of face, hands, head and feet that Muslims do before prayer
a building where Muslims pray together; in Arabic, masjid

look.title: How to Wash
look.text: You who believe, when you get up to pray, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. If you cannot find water, then use clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. God does not want to make things hard for you, but wants to make you clean.
look.cite: Qur'an 5:6, Al-Ma'idah, paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation (1930)
look.prompt: List the four parts of the body the ayah names. What does it say to do if there is no water?

check.q: What is wudu?
check.why: Wudu is the washing of face, hands, head and feet before prayer, described in 5:6.

check.q: What does the Arabic word masjid mean?
check.why: Masjid, the word for mosque, means a place of bowing down.

check.q: Which of these would you NOT find inside a mosque?
check.why: Mosques have no statues; the floor is carpet, an arch shows the qibla and shoes come off at the door.

lessons.title: Friday Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: On Fridays Muslims gather at midday for a talk and a prayer, as Surah 62:9 tells them to do.
reading: Friday is a special day for Muslims. Surah 62:9 says that when the call to prayer is given on Friday, people should leave their buying and selling and hurry to remember God. The surah is even named Al-Jumu'ah, "Friday" or "the gathering."

At midday on Friday, Muslims gather at the mosque. A leader called the *imam* gives a short talk, the *khutbah*. Then everyone prays together in rows. The next ayah, 62:10, says that after the prayer people may go back out and go about their work.

For Jews the special day is Saturday, the Sabbath. For most Christians it is Sunday. For Muslims it is Friday, but it is not a full day of rest in the Qur'an. In many Muslim countries, though, Friday is a day off from school and work.

words.d: the person who leads the prayer in a mosque and often gives the Friday talk
the short talk given before the Friday midday prayer

look.title: Three Special Days
look.text: Jews keep Saturday, the Sabbath, as a day of rest, following the Torah. Most Christians gather on Sunday, the day they believe Jesus rose. Muslims gather at midday on Friday, following Surah 62:9, and then go back to work. Three neighbors on one street might each have a different special day.
look.prompt: How are the three days alike? How is the Muslim Friday different from the Jewish Sabbath?

check.q: Which surah is named for Friday, the day of gathering?
check.why: Surah 62 is Al-Jumu'ah, meaning Friday or the gathering; 62:9 tells Muslims to hurry to prayer.

check.q: What is the khutbah?
choices: The short talk before the Friday prayer
The last month of the year
check.why: The khutbah is the short talk the imam gives before the Friday midday prayer.

check.q: What does 62:10 say people may do after the Friday prayer?
choices: Stay in the mosque all day
Go back out and go about their work
check.why: 62:10 says that after the prayer people may spread out in the land and seek God's bounty, that is, go back to work.

lessons.title: Two Eids
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims have two main holidays: Eid al-Fitr at the end of Ramadan and Eid al-Adha at the time of the hajj.
reading: *Eid* means "festival" or "holiday." Muslims have two big ones each year. The first is Eid al-Fitr, "the festival of breaking the fast." It comes the day after Ramadan ends. Families dress in new clothes, pray together in the morning and share sweets.

The second is Eid al-Adha, "the festival of the sacrifice." It comes about ten weeks later, at the end of the hajj. Muslims all over the world join in, not just the pilgrims in Mecca. It remembers Ibrahim (Abraham). The Qur'an says he was ready to give up his son for God (37:102–107).

On Eid al-Adha many families give meat to the poor and to neighbors. On both Eids, people say "Eid Mubarak." It means "blessed holiday." The dates move about eleven days earlier each year. That is because the Muslim calendar follows the moon.

words.d: a Muslim holiday; the two main ones are Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha
giving up something you value; Eid al-Adha remembers Ibrahim's readiness to give up his son

look.title: A Muslim Year on the Moon
rows: Days in a moon month, about
Days in the Muslim year, about
Days in the calendar year, about
Days the Eids move earlier each year, about
look.cite: Standard figures for the Islamic (Hijri) lunar calendar; U.S. Naval Observatory data on lunar months
look.prompt: If Eid al-Fitr was on April 1 this year, about when would it be next year?

check.q: When is Eid al-Fitr?
choices: On the first Friday of the year
In the middle of the hajj
check.why: Eid al-Fitr, the festival of breaking the fast, comes the day after Ramadan ends.

check.q: Which prophet does Eid al-Adha remember?
check.why: Eid al-Adha remembers Ibrahim, who the Qur'an says was ready to give up his son (37:102–107).

check.q: Why do the Eids come about eleven days earlier each year?
choices: The Muslim calendar follows the moon
The Qur'an lists a new date each year
check.why: The Muslim year follows the moon and is about eleven days shorter than the calendar year.

lessons.title: Halal Food
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an allows most foods, forbids a few, and Muslims call what is allowed halal.
reading: *Halal* means "allowed." *Haram* means "not allowed." The Qur'an says most foods are good to eat. Surah 2:172 tells believers to eat the good things God has given them and to give thanks. Then 2:173 gives a short list of what is not allowed.

The list includes meat from an animal that died on its own, blood, pork and meat offered to idols. Surah 5:3 gives a fuller list. Surah 5:90 tells Muslims to stay away from wine and other strong drink. Surah 5:5 says the food of the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, is allowed.

Many Muslims look for a halal label on meat. It means the animal was killed in the way Muslim tradition sets out, with God's name said. Jews have similar rules called kosher. In Chicago, many stores and restaurants sell halal food, and some school lunches offer it too.

words.d: allowed; food and actions that Muslims may have or do
not allowed; food and actions that Muslims may not have or do

look.title: A Short List
look.text: You who believe, eat the good things We have given you, and give thanks to God, if it is truly God you serve. God has forbidden you only this: animals that died on their own, blood, the flesh of pigs, and anything offered to any other than God. But whoever is forced by need, without wanting it and without going too far, does no wrong. God is forgiving and merciful.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:172–173, Al-Baqarah, paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation (1930)
look.prompt: What four things does the passage forbid? What does it say about a person who has no other food?

check.q: What does halal mean?
check.why: Halal means allowed; haram means not allowed.

check.q: Which of these does 2:173 say is NOT allowed?
check.why: 2:173 forbids animals that died on their own, blood, pork and meat offered to idols.

check.q: What does the Qur'an say about the food of Jews and Christians (5:5)?
check.why: Surah 5:5 says the food of the People of the Book is allowed to Muslims.

sections.title: A Day, a Year, a World

lessons.title: A Muslim Child's Day and Year
lessons.mainIdea: For many Muslim children the pillars shape each day and each year, in ways that differ from family to family.
reading: Take a boy named Idris, age nine, in Illinois. His day starts before sunrise. His mother prays the dawn prayer; he sometimes joins her, sometimes sleeps. At school he eats lunch that is halal. After school he prays the afternoon prayer at home, then plays basketball.

On Saturdays Idris goes to a class at the mosque to learn to read Arabic and memorize short surahs. On Fridays his father goes to the mosque at lunchtime. Some of Idris's Muslim friends do all these things. Some do a few. Families choose in their own ways.

His year has its own shape. Ramadan comes and the family eats iftar together every evening. Then Eid al-Fitr, with new clothes and gifts. About ten weeks later, Eid al-Adha. Some years his family sends money so a cousin can make the hajj. Each year the dates come a little earlier.

words.d: to learn something by heart so you can say it without looking
the things a person does in the same way each day or week

look.title: One Day of Prayer
look.cite: The five daily prayers as named in Muslim tradition (hadith collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim); times set by the sun
look.prompt: Which prayers would fall during a school day in Chicago in winter? Which in summer, when the sun sets late?

check.q: What does memorize mean?
check.why: To memorize is to learn by heart; many Muslim children memorize short surahs.

check.q: Which prayer comes first in the day?
check.why: Fajr is the dawn prayer, before sunrise; Isha is the last, at night.

check.q: Which sentence is TRUE about Muslim families and the pillars?
choices: Every family does exactly the same things
Families choose in their own ways; some do more, some do fewer
Children must fast all of Ramadan
check.why: Families differ; the Qur'an itself excuses children, the sick and travelers from fasting.

lessons.title: Muslims in Chicago and the World
lessons.mainIdea: About 1.9 billion people are Muslim, in every part of the world, and Chicago has a large, varied Muslim community.
reading: About one in four people on Earth is Muslim. Common estimates say around 1.9 billion; estimates vary. Most Muslims do not live in Arab countries. The countries with the most Muslims are Indonesia, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, in Asia.

Muslims are not all alike. Most are *Sunni*. About one in ten is *Shia*. They share the Qur'an and the pillars, but differ on some history and some practices. Muslims speak hundreds of languages. Many learn Arabic only to read the Qur'an.

Chicago has one of the largest Muslim communities in the United States. There are mosques on the North Side, the South Side and in many suburbs. Families come from South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Bosnia and elsewhere, and many are African American Muslims whose families have been here for generations.

words.d: the largest group of Muslims; most Muslims in the world are Sunni
the second largest group of Muslims; about one in ten Muslims is Shia

look.title: Where Muslims Live
look.cite: Pew Research Center estimates, The Future of the Global Muslim Population (2011) and later updates; estimates vary
look.prompt: Which region has the most Muslims? Does that surprise you? Why might people guess a different region?

check.q: About how many Muslims are there in the world?
check.why: Common estimates put the world's Muslims at around 1.9 billion, about one in four people.

check.q: Which region has the most Muslims?
check.why: About six in ten of the world's Muslims live in Asia and the Pacific, in countries like Indonesia and Pakistan.

check.q: What do Sunni and Shia Muslims share?
choices: The Qur'an and the Five Pillars
check.why: Sunni and Shia Muslims share the Qur'an and the pillars but differ on some history and practices.

review.q: Which of these is NOT one of the Five Pillars?
review.why: The pillars are shahada, prayer, zakat, fasting and hajj; the Torah is the Jewish scripture.

choices: The direction of the Kaaba in Mecca
review.why: The qibla is the direction of prayer, toward the Kaaba, as 2:144 says.

review.q: Which ayah names Ramadan as the month the Qur'an came down?
review.why: 2:185 names Ramadan as the month of the Qur'an and tells those present to fast.

review.q: What does 3:97 say about the hajj?
choices: It is a duty for those who are able to make the trip
review.why: 3:97 says the journey to the House is a duty owed to God by those who can make it.
5:6 describes wudu: washing the face, hands, head and feet before prayer.

review.q: Which holiday comes right after Ramadan?
review.why: Eid al-Fitr, the festival of breaking the fast, comes the day after Ramadan ends.
Haram means not allowed; halal means allowed.

review.q: Where do most of the world's Muslims live?
review.why: About six in ten Muslims live in Asia and the Pacific, according to common estimates.
